toc.title: Sadness comes from the state of your body
Don't evaluate it: validate, normalize, permit
Do you have to grin and bear it?

blocks.p: A member of my community asked me a bunch of questions about sadness. Here's what she wrote:

"I experience waves of sadness over the holidays that are a bit more frequent and intense than the rest of the year. I understand sadness is part of being human and having emotions. How do we know if sadness is maybe subconsciously related to a trauma, or just natural, something to accept and let pass on its own? Am I correct in thinking that anchoring in safety would be okay, be helpful for sadness of any origin? Or are we to grin and bear natural sadness (non-traumatically induced) via cognitive acceptance? Or is it really best to develop tolerance for all feelings of sadness via safety anchors?"
Lots of questions here, all around sadness. Let's break them down one by one.

blocks.h: Sadness comes from the state of your body

blocks.p: Yes, sadness is part of being human, or I guess part of being a mammal. It's an emotion that we have. But sadness is not random. It doesn't come out of nowhere. I don't think we're simply born feeling sad and therefore we'll be sad and depressed the rest of our lives. I haven't seen that in my clinical work as a therapist. Emotions don't pop up out of nowhere. They come from the state of our body.

If our body is in a state where it's prepared for danger, like flight or fight, our emotions are going to be flavored by that. They're going to be more anxious, maybe more aggressive. If our body's in a shutdown state, we're going to have more sadness and depression and numbness and loneliness. If our body's in more of a freeze state, we're going to have emotions of panic, maybe even explosive rage, overwhelm, stress.

If we can change the state of our body, our emotions change as well. But changing the state of the body first is not easy. The way I work as a therapist, the way I work on myself, and the way I teach, is kind of in reverse: we start with our emotions and then work backward toward the state.

If we can notice our emotions, like sadness, we can start to notice what's happening underneath those emotions, which are sensations and impulses. If we can feel those, mindfully experience them, and even act on them, the state of our body can change. If we can notice the sensations and impulses underneath the emotions of shutdown, for example, that can help us come out of shutdown, at least little by little. We can come out of shutdown into fight, and then flight, and then safety. But every step of the way, we have to notice what's happening within us on an emotional level.
Saying "I'm sad" is okay. I'm glad that you can recognize that. But then the question is: what does your sadness feel like? How do you know you're sad? How can you tell?
So that's the first part. Sadness is part of being human. It's not random. Our emotions are there for a reason. They come from the state of our body, and sadness comes from shutdown.

blocks.h: Don't evaluate it: validate, normalize, permit

blocks.p: Then she asked how we know if sadness is subconsciously related to a trauma. I would say: let's not evaluate it.
With my clients, in therapy and coaching, I have a three-step process.

ol: Validate it. Can you name it? Can you recognize what's true? Do you feel sadness? Yes. That's validation. You're just naming it. You're not dismissing it, you're not minimizing it. You're just saying, "This is true. I feel sad." All right, cool. Check.

Normalize it. Ask yourself: does it make sense why I feel sad? The answer could be, "It makes sense that I feel sad because something horrible just happened," or "because I've felt depressed for years." It could be, "I feel sad, and that's connected to some horrible stuff I went through as a kid," or "that's connected to my parents never building a healthy attachment with me." The question isn't whether it's good or bad. It's whether it makes sense. I think a lot of people might say no. So let me put it this way: if I had your life and I felt sad, would that make sense to you? Would you say to me, "Yeah, I get it. I can see why you feel sad"?
Give it permission. If you can name it, and it makes sense why it's there, can you give it permission to be there?

blocks.p: None of this involves evaluating whether this is a trauma sadness, a life context sadness, or a seasonal sadness. It's just sadness. Can you be with your sadness without judging it, without evaluating it? It's there. It's real. It makes sense why it's there. Now give it permission to be there, if you can handle it. If you can't, that's fine. Don't.

The way I work is very much present-moment focused. My focus is on what's happening now. What are you currently feeling, and can we let it be there? Especially, can we let it be there while anchored in safety?

That's her next question: is anchoring in safety okay, and helpful for sadness of any origin? Of course. It's always okay to anchor in your safety state. And to allow yourself to feel sadness, or other emotions that come from a defensive state, you kind of have to be anchored in safety.

If you feel sad without safety, then it's just sadness. You'll probably isolate in the dark. Maybe you'll reject people. But if you have access to your safety state, you can allow yourself to feel sadness with compassion. You can allow yourself to feel sadness with curiosity.

Maybe you'll still be by yourself, but it won't be in the dark, in the closet, isolating and rejecting the world. It'll be more like recognizing, "I need to be alone," and giving yourself solitude. It might be saying, "I need to be immobile. I need to be still. I need to just be, and have low stimulation." So you put on the right lighting, or the right kind of music for you, or just quiet. I need to be alone, I need to be still, I need the right kind of environment, and that's just what I need, without judgment or evaluation.
That's different from "I'm terrible. I'm horrible. I have to hide in my house with the lights off and ignore people." That's isolation. That's more like dysregulated sadness.

The sadness from safety has a much different look to it, with a lot more self-compassion. They both involve sadness, and they both stem from the polyvagal state of shutdown. But sadness without safety is dysregulated shutdown. Sadness with safety is regulated shutdown: safety plus shutdown. That allows the shutdown to be there, but with all the self-compassion.

blocks.h: Do you have to grin and bear it?

blocks.p: She also asked whether we're supposed to grin and bear natural sadness. I don't know if she means it this way, but to me that sounds like dysregulated sadness, where we're white-knuckling it. We're tensing our way through it, and there's no compassion and no curiosity.

Look, if you need to do that to get through the moment, that's fine. I'm not going to judge you. If you need to get through your sadness by some sort of coping, like distracting yourself, okay. Sometimes you might need to, especially when it's more the dysregulated flavor of sadness. But ideally, no, we don't want to just grin and bear it.

The same goes for "cognitive acceptance," if that means accepting, "Hey, I'm sad and I have to deal with it." That's just dealing with it, and that's fine. But it's not anchoring in safety, allowing yourself to feel it, and actually climbing your [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system).

The ideal is something much different. The ideal is that you're truly anchored in your safety state, and then you can choose to allow the sadness, to allow the shutdown to be there, from your safety state. That's the order I teach it in: first we learn how to anchor in safety. Then we learn how to anchor in safety and mindfully, compassionately allow the defensive state activation. We start with emotions like sadness, and then we work our way down to sensations and impulses.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: Her last question was whether it's best to develop tolerance for all feelings of sadness through safety anchors. Yes, I think so.

Sadness is sadness, but it can have different flavors. One person might say "I'm sad," and someone else might say "I'm sad," and they might not mean the same thing. The first person's sadness might be flavored by loneliness that's more about abandonment. The second person's might be flavored by rejection. They're both sad, they're both lonely, but the flavoring is different.

Whatever the sadness is, you can first anchor in safety, and then mindfully, compassionately choose to allow it. It won't be dysregulated at that point. It should be a healthier, more regulated experience. And if you can do that, you can eventually work your way down and notice the sensations and impulses underneath.
